case_name: Sumit Bansal v. MGI Developers and Promoters
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that where multiple cheques issued in connection with a single underlying transaction are dishonoured on different dates and followed by separate statutory notices, each dishonoured cheque gives rise to a distinct, independent cause of action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - multiple complaints arising from the same transaction are not, by that fact alone, an abuse of process.
why_it_matters: Payees holding several post-dated or instalment cheques from the same debtor can pursue a separate Section 138 complaint for each dishonoured cheque without risking a challenge that the multiplicity of complaints is itself vexatious.

case_name: Kaveri Plastics v. Mahdoom Bawa Bahrudeen Noorul
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act complaint where the statutory demand notice sought Rs. 2 crore although the dishonoured cheque was for Rs. 1 crore, holding that a demand notice must claim the exact cheque amount and that even this kind of discrepancy is fatal to the complaint's maintainability.
why_it_matters: Drafting a Section 138 demand notice for anything other than the precise cheque amount, including by inadvertent error, can be fatal to the resulting criminal complaint, making careful notice drafting essential before initiating cheque-bounce proceedings.

case_name: Arenel Private Limited v. M/s. Aakash Packaging
holding_summary: A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held that an arbitral award that relies on irrelevant material or ignores relevant evidence on record violates fundamental principles of justice and can be set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, upholding a Single Judge's decision that had set aside part of a December 2019 award in a packaging-materials supply dispute for reliance on hearsay over the parties' own laboratory reports.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that Indian courts will look past an arbitrator's findings of fact where the award is shown to rest on irrelevant material or to have disregarded directly relevant documentary evidence such as contemporaneous lab reports - a useful precedent for parties challenging awards on the patent-illegality/fundamental-justice ground.

case_name: The Reporters Collective Trust & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi, issued notice on petitions challenging Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 - which amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act to create a blanket exemption for personal information - along with a related challenge to Section 36 of the DPDP Act and Rule 23 of the DPDP Rules empowering government to call for information from data fiduciaries. The Court referred the core constitutional questions to a larger Bench while declining to stay operation of the DPDP framework in the meantime.
why_it_matters: Public authorities, RTI applicants and data fiduciaries should treat the DPDP Act's blanket RTI exemption for personal information as fully operative for now, since the Supreme Court declined any interim stay, while a larger Bench reference on its constitutionality remains pending.

case_name: In Re: Functioning of State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions in Low-Pendency States (Suo Motu)
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 11 February 2026
holding_summary: A Bench led by the Chief Justice, with Justice Joymalya Bagchi, invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to direct that sitting High Court judges in States and Union Territories that have found it not viable to constitute full-fledged State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions - including Sikkim, Manipur, Goa, Mizoram, Nagaland, Himachal Pradesh, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Meghalaya - will hear pending consumer complaints and appeals, functioning as deemed Chairpersons of the State Commission for that purpose.
why_it_matters: Consumers and businesses with pending consumer appeals in low-pendency States and UTs that lack a functioning State Commission now have a clear route to have those matters heard by a designated High Court judge instead of waiting indefinitely for a commission to be constituted.

case_name: The Managing Director, KSRTC v. P. Chandramouli & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pankaj Mithal and Prasanna B. Varale held that amounts received by the dependants of a deceased accident victim under an employer-provided group insurance scheme or other independent contractual/social-security benefit cannot be deducted from the compensation awarded under the Motor Vehicles Act, since such benefits arise from a separate contractual relationship with no requisite nexus to statutory motor accident compensation.
why_it_matters: Claimants receiving employer-linked group insurance or similar benefits after a fatal motor accident can be assured those amounts will not be set off against their MACT compensation, preserving the full value of both entitlements.

case_name: C. Velusamy v. K. Indhera
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar held that an application under Section 29A(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to extend an arbitral tribunal's mandate is maintainable even after expiry of the statutory time limit under Sections 29A(1) and (3), and even where an award has already been rendered during the interim period. The Court noted that an award passed after the mandate has expired is unenforceable and non est, but that an arbitrator's error in passing such an award does not deprive the court of jurisdiction to entertain a later extension application.
why_it_matters: Parties whose arbitral tribunal issues an award after its Section 29A mandate has technically lapsed are not left without a remedy - they can still apply to extend the mandate after the fact, rather than being forced to restart arbitration from scratch.

case_name: Hindustan Unilever Limited v. Kwick Living (I) Private Limited
holding_summary: In HUL's disparagement and trademark suit over Kwick Living's comparative advertising campaign against Vim and Surf Excel, a Division Bench (Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani) held that principles of territorial jurisdiction are not diluted merely because allegedly infringing content is accessible over the internet across India. While deciding jurisdiction for the dispute before it, the Bench referred to a Larger Bench the broader questions of how Section 20 CPC, Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act, and Section 62 of the Copyright Act interact to fix jurisdiction for suits arising from online advertising and e-commerce sales.
why_it_matters: Until the Larger Bench rules, companies bringing or defending IP and comparative-advertising suits over online content can no longer assume they may sue wherever their goods or ads are digitally accessible; where the corporate plaintiff's registered office sits will remain a live jurisdictional question.

case_name: Kavitha Kuruganti v. PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran declined to revoke PepsiCo India's registration of its FL 2027 (FC-5) potato variety, used for Lay's chips, under Section 34(h) of the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, holding that having earlier sued (and then withdrawn suits against) Gujarat farmers for infringement did not itself justify revocation. The Court simultaneously held that individual farmers sued for using protected seed can invoke the statutory farmers' privilege under Section 39(1)(iv) of the PPVFR Act to save, use, sow, exchange or sell farm produce, including seed of a protected variety.
why_it_matters: Reportedly the first Supreme Court ruling construing the PPVFR Act's registration and farmers'-rights provisions together, giving seed/agri companies clarity that pursuing (even later-withdrawn) infringement suits will not itself void a variety's registration, while confirming farmers retain a statutory shield against such suits.

case_name: M/s Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation v. Central Board of Trustees & Anr.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, while resolving appeals over provident fund and gratuity dues owed to workmen in an insolvency-resolution context, referred to a larger Bench the question whether the authorised officer has discretion under Section 14B of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 to levy less than full damages for default, or whether imposition of maximum damages is mandatory. The Court directed EPF dues, together with Section 7Q interest, be paid in four quarterly instalments from December 2026.
why_it_matters: Employers facing EPF default penalties - including those emerging from insolvency resolution plans - now face an unsettled but live question on whether authorities must impose maximum Section 14B damages or retain discretion to moderate them, pending the larger Bench's ruling.

case_name: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II v. Ms. Mamta Binani & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu restored an NCLAT appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC that had been dismissed as time-barred, after the appellant's counsel made a bona fide attempt to e-file on the last day of limitation but could not because of a backend technical glitch in NCLAT's own e-filing portal, with the appeal actually filed only one day late. Invoking the principle that an act of the court should prejudice no one, the Court held the period during which the portal was non-functional could be excluded, and remitted the matter to NCLAT to decide afresh whether sufficient cause existed to condone any residual delay.
why_it_matters: Litigants who can show a genuine, timely attempt to e-file before an IBC appeal deadline now have Supreme Court authority to seek exclusion of time lost to a tribunal's own portal failure, rather than being shut out by NCLAT's otherwise strict 45-day limitation regime.

case_name: Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. & Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd. v. Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
citation: Appeal, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (judgment dated 17 September 2026)
holding_summary: A Bench of Judicial Member Virender Bhat and Technical Member Ajay Talegaonkar dismissed the appeal of Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. and group company Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd., upholding HERC's denial of 'captive user' status for power banked from Piccadily Agro's 17 MW biomass co-generation plant to the hotel unit, since Piccadily Hotels held only 14.57% equity in the generating company against the 26% minimum ownership threshold prescribed under the Electricity Rules, 2005. The Tribunal directed payment of outstanding banking-benefit dues of over Rs. 68 lakh to the discom.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that intra-group captive-power arrangements must strictly satisfy the 26% equity and 51% self-consumption thresholds under the Electricity Rules, or risk losing captive status - and associated open-access/cross-subsidy benefits - regardless of a power-banking agreement between group companies.

case_name: Koenig Solutions Pvt. Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner, Audit Branch
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court quashed a special-audit communication issued in Form GST ADT-03 and a consequential DRC-01 against Koenig Solutions for FY 2018-19, after the GST department conceded that no final order under Section 73 of the CGST Act had been passed by the statutory deadline of 30 April 2024. The Court held the audit process could not be kept alive indefinitely once the time limit for the underlying demand order had lapsed.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers facing open-ended GST special audits or notices tied to a financial year whose Section 73 limitation has already expired can rely on this ruling to have stale audit communications and demand notices quashed outright.

case_name: National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Co-location & Dark Fibre Settlement)
citation: Civil appeals arising from SAT order (disposed 18 September 2026)
holding_summary: The Supreme Court permitted a settlement between NSE and SEBI in the decade-old algorithmic-trading co-location and dark-fibre cases, under which NSE will pay approximately Rs. 1,491.21 crore under SEBI's settlement mechanism (Rs. 1,223.56 crore for co-location and Rs. 267.65 crore for the dark-fibre matter), disposing of SEBI's pending appeals against the Securities Appellate Tribunal's 2023 order that had earlier set aside SEBI's disgorgement direction.
why_it_matters: Brings finality to one of India's longest-running securities-market enforcement disputes and signals the Supreme Court's willingness to permit large-scale regulatory settlements even after years of SAT and appellate litigation - a template other market infrastructure institutions facing SEBI proceedings may look to.

case_name: Sai Consulting Engineers Pvt. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India & Ors.
citation: Delhi High Court, judgment dated 11 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sachin Datta quashed NHAI's two-year debarment of consultancy firm Sai Consulting Engineers from future bids - imposed over alleged breaches of a 2018 consultancy agreement for Detailed Project Reports on several bypass/ring-road projects - holding that an ordinary contractual breach unaccompanied by fraud or collusion cannot justify blacklisting. The debarment order was set aside while NHAI's right to separately claim damages for the alleged breach was expressly preserved.
why_it_matters: Reinforces the high threshold - fraud, collusion or moral turpitude, not mere contractual default - that government authorities like NHAI must meet before blacklisting a contractor or consultant, an important check for infrastructure-sector service providers facing debarment action.

case_name: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Trupti Sanjay Mehta & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva held that a bank can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to recover a secured loan it acquired by assignment from an NBFC, even though that NBFC was not a 'financial institution' covered by the Act at the time the loan was originally created, setting aside a Bombay High Court ruling that had restricted Kotak Mahindra Bank from enforcing SARFAESI against a loan portfolio it had acquired from City Financial Consumer Finance Ltd.
why_it_matters: Confirms that banks and ARCs acquiring loan books from non-SARFAESI-covered NBFCs and other lenders can still use SARFAESI's summary enforcement mechanism, removing significant legal uncertainty from the secondary loan-sale and securitisation market.

case_name: Nikhil Mehta & Anr. v. Gardenview Abode Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of President Justice A.P. Sahi and Member Bharatkumar Pandya declined to entertain a consumer complaint against the developer of Bengaluru's 'Mantri Blossom' project (formerly Mantri Developers, now Gardenview Abode) seeking a refund the complainants had already secured with interest from the Karnataka Real Estate Regulatory Authority for the same booking, applying the doctrine of election to bar parallel proceedings for the same relief, while leaving the complainants free to enforce the existing K-RERA order.
why_it_matters: Confirms that homebuyers who have already obtained an enforceable refund order from RERA cannot separately pursue an overlapping consumer complaint for the same relief, underscoring the need to choose one forum - RERA or the consumer commission - and see it through.

case_name: Havells India Limited & Anr. v. Havai Home Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: Justice Jyoti Singh held that a defendant's own trademark registration for 'HAVAI' is no defence to a passing-off action where the plaintiff shows prior goodwill in 'HAVELLS', deceptive similarity and likelihood of consumer confusion, and restrained Havai Home Products from using the 'HAVAI' word and device marks, or any other mark deceptively similar to the Havells marks, assessing passing off by reference to actual stylisation, colour scheme and market presentation rather than merely the registered form of the mark.
why_it_matters: Reaffirms for brand owners that obtaining a trademark registration for a deceptively similar mark does not immunise a junior user from a passing-off injunction, keeping the legal focus on actual marketplace conduct and consumer confusion rather than registry status.

case_name: Goyal Hariyana Realty v. Mrs. Vinaya & Ors.
court: Karnataka Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru
holding_summary: A Bench of Chairperson Justice J.M. Khazi and Judicial Member Santhosh Kumar Shetty N. dismissed a builder's appeal and upheld an order directing the builder and landowner to jointly pay Rs. 6 lakh as compensation to two homebuyers for construction defects, plus Rs. 5,000 in costs. The builder had argued that an earlier settlement deed between the parties barred the claim. The Tribunal held that the settlement deed's broad wording covered only disputes subsisting as of the date it was executed and could not be read as an unconditional waiver of claims arising from defects discovered by the allottees only after they took possession, since such later-discovered defects constitute a distinct cause of action.
why_it_matters: Builders cannot rely on broadly worded settlement deeds to shut out homebuyer claims for defects that surface after possession; developers should draft settlement/release clauses to expressly address post-possession defect liability if they intend to close that exposure.

case_name: Spherion Solutions Private Limited v. Additional Commissioner, Adjudication, CGST Delhi North & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain held that Input Tax Credit blocked under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules cannot itself satisfy the mandatory pre-deposit required under Section 107(6) of the CGST Act to file a GST appeal, since a Rule 86A restriction prevents the credit from being debited from the electronic credit ledger unless the restriction is first removed or modified by the competent authority. The Court nonetheless allowed the petitioner to pursue its statutory appeal.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers with ITC blocked under Rule 86A cannot rely on that blocked credit to meet a GST appeal's pre-deposit; they must arrange payment through other means or get the restriction lifted first.

case_name: M/s Aliens Developers Private Limited v. Telangana Real Estate Regulatory Authority & Anr.
court: Telangana Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad
holding_summary: A Bench of Chairperson Justice A. Santhosh Reddy, Judicial Member P. Pradeep Kumar Reddy and Administrative Member Vemula Sreekar upheld a Telangana RERA order directing Aliens Developers to refund the balance amount due to a homebuyer who had voluntarily cancelled her flat booking, holding that execution of a cancellation deed does not by itself terminate the buyer's status as an 'allottee' - that status continues until the developer actually pays the full agreed refund.
why_it_matters: Developers cannot treat a signed cancellation deed as closing out their refund obligations; buyers retain enforceable allottee rights, including RERA remedies, until they are paid in full.

case_name: Aayush Prashant Agarwal v. Uma Export Limited & Klass Insolvency Resolution Professionals Private Limited
citation: I.A. No. 5601 of 2026 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) 1366/2024; 2026 LLBiz NCLAT 338
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: The NCLAT Principal Bench permitted the Interim Resolution Professional of Epic Yarns Private Limited to move the NCLT for withdrawal of an admitted CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC, following a post-admission settlement between operational creditor Uma Export Limited and the corporate debtor, applying the withdrawal framework as substituted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2026.
why_it_matters: One of the first significant applications of the 2026 IBC amendment's tightened Section 12A regime, confirming that a genuine post-admission settlement can still support withdrawal so long as it is routed through the amended procedure and timing windows.

case_name: Spectrum Power Generation Limited v. GAIL (India) Limited
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court set aside an arbitral award that had rejected Spectrum Power Generation's claim for refund of GST reimbursed to GAIL (India) Limited on transmission charges under a Gas Sale Agreement, holding that the award was vitiated by patent illegality because it rested on inadmissible evidence and an erroneous application of the doctrines of waiver and estoppel.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that an arbitral tribunal's findings on waiver, estoppel and its treatment of evidence remain open to Section 34 scrutiny where they are perverse or legally unsound, giving parties a further avenue to challenge awards resting on flawed evidentiary reasoning.

case_name: National Seeds Corporation Ltd. v. National Agro Seed Corporation (India)
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that an award-debtor's liability to pay interest does not cease merely because the award amount is deposited in court; interest liability ends only where the deposit is made in accordance with Order XXI Rule 1 CPC, so that the award-holder can withdraw it unconditionally. The Court affirmed the Delhi High Court's direction to pay 12% annual interest for the period between the award and the eventual release of the deposited amount, and asked the Law Commission to examine a uniform framework for court deposits.
why_it_matters: Award-debtors who deposit funds in court to stop the interest clock must ensure the deposit is unconditional and Order XXI Rule 1-compliant, or they remain liable for interest despite having paid the money into court.

case_name: ITC Limited v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Ors.
citation: Delhi High Court, interim order dated 25 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma granted interim protection to ITC Limited, restraining FSSAI from cancelling its food business licence over advisories objecting to the '100% Atta', '100% Madhya Pradesh Wheat' and '0% Maida' claims on Aashirvaad MP Chakki Atta packaging, pending further hearing listed for 9 September 2026. The dispute traces to a May 2025 FSSAI advisory asking food business operators to stop using '100%' claims on labels.
why_it_matters: Food business operators facing FSSAI licence-cancellation action over labelling claims can seek interim court protection while the underlying dispute over permissible claims is adjudicated; the matter remains pending and its final outcome is unresolved.

case_name: In re: Procedure for Milestone Extension Charges for GNA Connectivity Grantees
holding_summary: The CERC approved a procedure for levying graded Milestone Extension Charges that allows renewable energy generators, storage systems and renewable power park developers who are behind schedule on land-document submission, Financial Closure or Commercial Operation Date milestones under the CERC (Connectivity and General Network Access) Regulations, 2022 to pay for additional time, replacing the earlier regime of automatic revocation of transmission connectivity for missed milestones.
why_it_matters: Renewable energy developers facing delay in meeting General Network Access milestones now have a structured, compensation-based path to retain scarce interstate transmission connectivity instead of losing it outright, though charges rise progressively with the length of the delay.

case_name: Rajat Sharma & Independent News Service Pvt. Ltd. v. Tamara Doc & Ors.
citation: Delhi High Court, decree dated 24 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Jyoti Singh granted a decree of permanent injunction in favour of India TV chairman Rajat Sharma and Independent News Service Pvt. Ltd. against several Facebook pages and two YouTube channels that had used AI-generated deepfake videos carrying distorted, modulated versions of Sharma's image and voice, restraining further infringement of his personality and publicity rights and misuse of India TV's registered trademarks, and directing Meta and Google to act on takedown requests within a set timeframe.
why_it_matters: Extends Delhi High Court personality-rights jurisprudence to combat AI-generated deepfake content, giving public figures a concrete remedy - including platform-directed takedown timelines - against unauthorised, AI-manipulated use of their image and voice.

case_name: U.P. State Highways Authority v. M/s Abhijeet Meerut Karnal Toll Road Limited
citation: Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench), judgment dated 23 July 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench partly allowed U.P. State Highways Authority's appeal against a 2017 arbitral award in a highway concession dispute, holding that a financial model based on assumptions cannot, by itself, quantify a claim for loss of profits, and set aside the Rs. 157.57 crore loss-of-profits component of the award while upholding the award's remaining findings, including the Rs. 25.53 crore award for EPC-contractor payments, and remitting the loss-of-profits claim to a freshly constituted arbitral tribunal.
why_it_matters: Concessionaires pursuing loss-of-profits claims in infrastructure arbitrations should note that financial-model-based quantification alone may not survive Section 34 scrutiny, and that only the flawed head of a mixed award - not the entire award - may be severed and remitted.

case_name: Tirupati Devi Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s Raja Construction Company & Ors.
citation: NCDRC, New Delhi, order dated 17 August 2026
holding_summary: A Bench of President Justice A.P. Sahi and Member Bharatkumar Pandya held that a builder's handing over of possession without obtaining the Occupation Certificate, and constructing beyond the sanctioned plan, constitutes a continuing deficiency in service, in a nearly two-decade-old Mumbai redevelopment dispute. The Commission directed the builder to obtain the Occupation Certificate within 12 months, pay the complainant society Rs. 6 crore, and pay Rs. 10 lakh in litigation costs.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a developer's failure to secure an Occupation Certificate is treated as an ongoing, not time-barred, deficiency in service, giving housing societies and flat owners a continuing cause of action even many years after possession was handed over.

case_name: Srinivasa Reddy Velagala v. Sravanthi Infratech Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that a Section 9 IBC application based on an EPC contract for a 225 MW gas-based power station was time-barred, since the operational creditor's claims had crystallised around 2011-2012 but the insolvency application was filed only in 2018. The Court clarified that the mere subsistence of an underlying contract does not create a continuing cause of action or indefinitely extend limitation once a default has occurred.
why_it_matters: Operational creditors can no longer assume that an ongoing or subsisting contract keeps their right to seek insolvency alive; claims must be pursued within three years of the actual default, not the eventual termination of the relationship.

case_name: Tata Capital Financial Services Limited v. Neel Motors LLP & Ors.
holding_summary: Justice Somasekhar Sundaresan held that the amendment inserting Section 96(4) of the IBC, effective 26 May 2026, which excludes personal guarantors of corporate debtors from the interim moratorium under Section 96, applies to Section 95 applications that were already pending as of that date. The Court reasoned that the statutory phrase 'where an application is filed' covers anything filed and still pending on the effective date, so the change operates retroactively (not merely prospectively).
why_it_matters: Lenders pursuing personal guarantors in pending Section 95 proceedings can now invoke parallel remedies such as arbitration or SARFAESI without waiting for those insolvency applications to conclude, since the automatic moratorium no longer shields guarantors mid-proceeding.

case_name: M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited, Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court set aside a Section 74 CGST/MPGST show cause notice issued for AY 2018-19, holding that beyond a bare assertion of 'fraud or concealment of facts' the notice disclosed no underlying facts or circumstances from which fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression could be inferred. The Court reiterated that the extended limitation period under Section 74 cannot be invoked through mechanical recitals of the statutory language alone.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers facing Section 74 notices issued after the ordinary Section 73 limitation period has lapsed now have clear Supreme Court authority to challenge notices that merely recite 'fraud' or 'suppression' without pleading specific supporting facts.

case_name: M/s Aims Max Gardenia Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. Mrs. Pratibha Gupta
holding_summary: The Allahabad High Court dismissed a builder's appeal seeking condonation of a 721-day delay in filing, holding that unexplained inaction and oversight do not amount to 'sufficient cause,' and upheld the RERA authority's order directing immediate possession of a Sector-75 Noida flat to the homebuyer with interest at 24% per annum (the same rate the builder-buyer agreement itself prescribed against a defaulting buyer). The Court also imposed Rs. 2.5 lakh in costs on the builder for putting the homebuyer through roughly 13 years of litigation.
why_it_matters: Developers cannot rely on vague claims of oversight to excuse long delays in appealing RERA orders, and courts will hold builders to the same interest rate their own agreements impose on defaulting buyers, with costs for prolonged, vexatious litigation.

case_name: Prabhat Kumar Singh & Ors. v. Accu Pack Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
citation: Supreme Court of India, Bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that under Section 4(6) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employer's right to forfeit gratuity of an employee terminated for misconduct causing loss is limited strictly to the loss actually proved, rejecting the employer's claim of a Rs. 50 lakh loss for lack of independent evidence such as an audit report. The Court restored the Controlling Authority's original order allowing the employees' gratuity claims, setting aside contrary findings of the Appellate Authority and the High Court.
why_it_matters: Employers seeking to withhold gratuity on grounds of employee misconduct must substantiate the exact quantum of loss with credible evidence; bare allegations of financial damage will not justify forfeiting an employee's statutory gratuity entitlement.

case_name: Rukhmani Keshwani (trading as Vishwas Agarbatti Store) v. Raju Agarbatti Works & Anr.
citation: Delhi High Court, Division Bench order
holding_summary: A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court restored a trademark and copyright infringement suit over the 'RADHEY KRISHNA' agarbatti mark between two Rajasthan-based manufacturers, holding that a trial court had wrongly returned the plaint for want of territorial jurisdiction. The Court found that listings for the defendant's goods accessible and purchasable in Delhi via the IndiaMart online marketplace were sufficient to confer territorial jurisdiction on the Delhi courts.
why_it_matters: Businesses selling through interactive e-commerce and B2B marketplace platforms can be sued for IP infringement in any jurisdiction where their listings are accessible and goods can be purchased, significantly widening the range of forums available to plaintiffs in online trademark disputes.

case_name: Kirloskar Ferrous Industries Ltd. & Anr. v. Union of India & Anr.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan upheld the constitutional validity of the Explanation to Rule 38 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 2016 and Rule 45(8)(a) of the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 2017, which require royalty, DMF and NMET payments to be included in the sale value used to compute the Average Sale Price of iron ore for royalty purposes. The Court rejected the argument that this amounts to an impermissible 'royalty on royalty' and held the rules are not violative of Articles 14 or 19(1)(g).
why_it_matters: Iron ore miners cannot exclude statutory royalty, DMF and NMET contributions from the sale value used to compute their own royalty liability, confirming a higher effective royalty base than industry had argued for.

case_name: Steel Authority of India Limited v. British Marine PLC
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Prathiba M. Singh and Vikas Mahajan dismissed SAIL's challenge to an arbitral award in favour of British Marine, rejecting SAIL's argument that two tribunal members were disqualified merely because they had previously interpreted the same contractual clause (Clause 62) in a separate maritime arbitration involving SAIL. The Court held that such 'issue conflict' does not by itself give rise to justifiable doubts about independence or impartiality under Section 12 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, and upheld the tribunal's damages assessment based on the differential between contract and spot market freight rates.
why_it_matters: Parties in specialised sectors like shipping and commodities, where the pool of experienced arbitrators is limited, cannot automatically disqualify an arbitrator simply because they previously ruled on the same standard clause in an unrelated dispute.

case_name: In re: Simbhaoli Sugars Limited (Gursimran Kaur Mann v. Financial Creditor & Ors.)
citation: NCLAT, New Delhi (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency)), order dated 13 July 2026
holding_summary: The NCLAT dismissed an appeal by promoter Gursimran Kaur Mann and disposed of a related appeal by a sugarcane farmer creditor, vacating all interim stays and clearing the way for Simbhaoli Sugars' CIRP (pending since July 2024, with outstanding debt of about Rs. 1,436.92 crore) to proceed. The Tribunal rejected the argument that the insolvency was triggered only by the RBI's since-struck-down 12 February 2018 circular, finding the financial creditor had already initiated recovery and recalled the loan before that circular issued, and directed the Resolution Professional to duly consider sugarcane farmers' statutory dues (reported at about Rs. 487 crore) in the resolution process.
why_it_matters: Confirms that sugar mills cannot escape CIRP by blaming a now-invalidated RBI circular where recovery action predated it, while signalling that farmers' cane-price dues must be factored into the resolution process even as insolvency proceeds.
